newsitem.title: USA: World groups too bullish on food security - report.
newsitem.headline: World groups too bullish on food security - report.

text.p: An independent study group on Saturday called on world bodies to take a more pessimistic view of dwindling world food supplies at the U.N. World Food Summit in Rome next month.
Both the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Bank were guilty of overestimating world food production over the next decade-and-a-half, the Worldwatch Institute said.
"The demand, driven by population -- especially in Asia -- is simply outstripping the supply of food," Worldwatch president Lester Brown said.

In a report intended to contribute to the debate in Rome, Worldwatch said both the FAO and the World Bank had simply projected that world grain production would continue to grow from 1990 to 2010 at the same rate it had in the previous 40 years.
Both groups have said grain production will grow by about 25 million metric tons a year, to 2.3 billion in 2010 from 1.8 billion in 1990.

But Worldwatch said harvests in the first half of the 1990s had shown grain production was growing by a much smaller amount. Early estimates by the U.S. Department of Agriculture put the 1996 harvest at 1.82 billion tons.
Brown said the FAO and the World Bank should replace their economists with interdisciplinary teams that can analyse new forces, such as global warming, water scarcity and population.

"Food scarcity is emerging as the defining issue of a new era, much as ideolgical conflict was the defining issue in the era that recently ended," Brown said, referring to ideological conflict between capitalism and communism.

In a May 31 letter to Worldwatch, World Bank President James Wolfensohn said the bank was preparing a new statement on long-term food security prospects ahead of the FAO food summit, which starts on November 13.
